title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
pattern: Hash Map with Index Tracking + Swap-Remove
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> vals: up to n elements → O(n)
- unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>> mp: total of n indices stored across all keys → O(n)
- recursion depth: none
- not counted: input, returned int
approach: Store all elements (with duplicates) in a vector `vals` for O(1) random access. Maintain an `unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>>` mapping each value to the set of indices where it appears in `vals`. Insert pushes to the back and records the index. Remove picks any index of `val`, swaps it with the last element, then fixes up the index sets for both the removed value and the swapped-in last value (carefully handling the case where the removed element is itself the last one). getRandom indexes `vals` at a uniform random position, giving probability proportional to multiplicity. All operations are O(1) average.
hints: If every element sits in a flat list for uniform sampling, what extra information would let you find and delete one copy of a given value in O(1) without shifting?

Use a vector to store all elements and a hash map from value to a set of indices. After `insert(1), insert(1), insert(2)`, the vector is `[1,1,2]` and the map is `{1→{0,1}, 2→{2}}`. To remove, pick any index of the value, swap it with the last element, update both index sets, and pop.

```
insert(val):
  map[val].add(vector.size)
  vector.push(val)
  return map[val] was empty before

remove(val):
  if map[val] is empty: return false
  i = any index from map[val]
  last = vector.back
  vector[i] = last
  map[val].erase(i)
  map[last].insert(i)
  map[last].erase(vector.size - 1)
  vector.pop
  return true

getRandom():
  return vector[rand % vector.size]
```

**Stale index after swap** - the removed value is not the last element, so its old index now holds a different value
`Input: ["RandomizedCollection","insert","insert","remove","remove"], [[],[1],[2],[1],[1]]` → `Expected: [null,true,true,true,false]`
⚠️ Bug: not erasing the old index from map[val] after swapping → map[1] retains index 0, so the second remove(1) returns true and pops from an already-shrunk vector.

**Empty set, key persists** - all copies of a value are removed but the map key remains with an empty set
`Input: ["RandomizedCollection","insert","remove","remove"], [[],[3],[3],[3]]` → `Expected: [null,true,true,false]`
⚠️ Bug: checking only `map.count(val) > 0` without checking set emptiness → begin() is dereferenced on an empty set (undefined behavior) instead of returning false.

**Wrong erase order when val equals last** - removing the last element which is the only copy of its value, then inserting a different value at the freed index
`Input: ["RandomizedCollection","insert","insert","remove","insert","remove"], [[],[1],[2],[2],[3],[2]]` → `Expected: [null,true,true,true,true,false]`
⚠️ Bug: erasing vec.size()-1 from map[last] before inserting i when val==last and i==vec.size()-1 → the index is re-added after erasure, so map[2] retains a stale index and the final remove(2) returns true instead of false.

followUps.q: What if each distinct value has a custom weight and getRandom must return a value with probability proportional to weight × count?
followUps.a: Replace the flat vector with a Fenwick tree over cumulative weights. Insert/remove updates the weight at the value's slot; getRandom binary-searches for a random target in the cumulative sum. TC: O(log U) per operation where U is the number of distinct values; SC: O(U).

followUps.q: What if the collection must support countInRange(lo, hi) returning the number of elements with values in [lo, hi] in O(1)?
followUps.a: Replace the hash map with a Fenwick tree indexed by value domain. Each insert/remove increments/decrements the count at that value's position; countInRange is two prefix-sum queries. TC: O(log V) for insert/remove/count where V is the value range; SC: O(V).

followUps.q: What if the collection is distributed across multiple machines and must support all three operations?
followUps.a: Use consistent hashing to assign each value to a shard; each shard maintains its own vector and index map. getRandom picks a shard proportional to its element count, then samples locally. TC: O(1) plus network round-trip; SC: O(n) total across shards.
